title: Dog Hot Spots: How to Stop Acute Moist Dermatitis From Spreading
description: Hot spots on dogs can double in size overnight. Learn the causes, at-home first steps, and when to call your vet before it spreads.
content:
That Wet, Angry Patch on Your Dog's Hip Isn't Just a Scratch

Two summers ago my neighbor's golden retriever, Max, went from fine at breakfast to a golf-ball-sized oozing sore on his flank by dinner. She thought he'd been stung by something. By the next morning it was the size of her palm. That's a hot spot — acute moist dermatitis — and if you've never dealt with one, the speed is genuinely alarming. These lesions can expand an inch or more in a few hours, and the smell hits you before you even see it. I've watched owners waste two days trying coconut oil and vet wraps while the infection tunneled deeper into the skin.

Here's the thing nobody tells you at the pet store: hot spots are almost never the real problem. They're a symptom. The dog itches, chews, or scratches a spot raw, bacteria that already live on the skin (usually Staphylococcus pseudintermedius) move in, and the dog's immune response creates a self-perpetuating cycle of itch-scratch-itch. Stop the cycle fast and you win. Wait, and you're looking at a vet bill, antibiotics, and a cone for two weeks.

According to the American Veterinary Medical Association, skin conditions — including hot spots — are among the top reasons dogs visit the vet each year. So this isn't a rare edge case. It's one of the most common things you'll face as a dog owner.

What Exactly Is a Hot Spot?

The medical term is acute moist dermatitis, and the name is dead accurate. Acute means it comes on fast. Moist means it weeps. Dermatitis means inflamed skin. Vets sometimes call it pyotraumatic dermatitis if there's pus involved, which there usually is.

What you'll see: a well-defined, red, raw patch that's often wet with serum or pus. The hair over it is usually matted and stuck to the skin. Your dog will lick, chew, or scratch at it obsessively. It smells yeasty or frankly foul. It's painful — dogs will flinch when you touch it, and some get snappy about it. My own shepherd mix, Roo, snapped at me once when I tried to move the fur aside to look. She'd never done that before or since. That's how much these hurt.

Where they show up: anywhere the dog can reach. That means the hip, the flank, the base of the tail, the side of the face, the neck under the collar, and the outer ear. Long-haired breeds with dense undercoats — goldens, huskies, Newfoundlands, Saint Bernards — get them worse because moisture gets trapped against the skin and the fur hides the early stages until it's big.

The Real Causes (and Why 'Just Allergies' Is Only Half the Answer)

Anything that makes a dog itch can kick off a hot spot. But some triggers are far more common than others.

Flea allergy dermatitis. This is the number one cause in many dogs, especially in summer. A single flea bite on a flea-allergic dog can cause itching for days. The classic location is the lower back and tail base — exactly where hot spots love to form.

Environmental allergies. Pollen, grass, mold spores. Dogs with atopic dermatitis scratch and chew seasonally. Spring and fall are peak hot spot season for these dogs.

Food allergies. Less common than people think, but real. Usually accompanied by year-round itching, ear infections, and GI upset.

Ear infections. A dog with an infected ear will scratch at it constantly. The scratch creates a hot spot on the side of the face or the ear flap. If your dog has a hot spot near the ear, get the ear checked — you may be treating the wrong thing.

Anal gland problems. Dogs with impacted or infected anal glands scoot and chew at the tail base. Same story.

Moisture and poor grooming. A dog who swims daily and never gets dried properly, or a thick-coated dog in humid weather, is a hot spot waiting to happen. Matting traps moisture and pulls at the skin, which starts the itch.

Boredom and stress. Under-exercised dogs sometimes lick compulsively. It's a displacement behavior, and it creates the same lesion.

Notice the pattern? The hot spot is the visible end of a chain that started somewhere else. Treat the spot without treating the trigger and it comes back. I've seen dogs on their fourth hot spot in two months because the owner kept buying topical spray instead of figuring out why the dog was itching.

What to Do in the First Hour

Speed matters more than anything else here. If you catch a hot spot when it's the size of a quarter, you can often manage it at home with a call to your vet. If it's the size of a silver dollar or bigger, or it's already oozing pus, call the vet before you do anything else.

Here's the at-home protocol vets generally recommend for small, early spots:

1. Clip the fur around the lesion. Not shave — clip. You want to expose the skin and let air get to it. Use blunt-nosed grooming clippers and go slowly. If the spot is painful, your dog may not tolerate this. Don't force it. A groomer or vet tech can do it in five minutes if you can't.

2. Clean gently with a dilute antiseptic. Chlorhexidine solution (the kind sold for veterinary use, typically 2 to 4 percent) diluted per the label, or plain saline. Don't use hydrogen peroxide — it damages healthy tissue and slows healing. Don't use alcohol — it stings like crazy. I keep a bottle of vet-strength chlorhexidine wipes in my dog kit. They're cheap and they work. Here's one I've used: chlorhexidine antiseptic wipes for dogs.

3. Pat dry. Don't rub. Rubbing spreads bacteria and irritates the skin further.

4. Prevent the dog from reaching it. This is non-negotiable. An Elizabethan collar, a soft recovery cone, or a surgical suit — whatever your dog tolerates. If they can still reach the spot, everything else you do is wasted. I've seen dogs lick through a bandage. A cone is not optional.

5. Call your vet. Even if it looks small. They may want to prescribe a topical antibiotic-steroid combination, an oral antibiotic, or a short course of steroids to break the itch cycle. Hot spots that are infected need antibiotics. No home remedy substitutes for that.

What not to do: don't apply human hydrocortisone cream (dogs lick it off and it's not formulated for them), don't use tea tree oil (toxic to dogs in sufficient quantities), don't wrap the spot in a bandage that traps moisture, and don't wait to see if it gets better on its own. It won't.

Vet Treatment: What to Expect

Your vet will do a skin cytology — basically a tape prep or scraping examined under a microscope — to confirm what's growing. If it's a straightforward bacterial hot spot, the typical protocol is:

Clipping and cleaning of the area, often with the dog sedated if it's large or painful.

Topical treatment, usually a combination product with an antibiotic, an antifungal, and a steroid. Brands like Animax, Gentocin, or Mupirocin ointment. Applied two to three times daily for one to two weeks.

Oral antibiotics for 7 to 21 days if the infection is deep or widespread. Cephalexin is the workhorse. Finish the whole course even if it looks healed in five days. Stopping early is how you breed resistant bacteria.

Oral steroids or Apoquel to shut down the itch. This is the part that stops the cycle. Without it, the dog keeps scratching and the spot keeps growing.

Flea control, if fleas are involved. Prescription preventatives are far more effective than over-the-counter products. According to the FDA, some OTC flea products have been linked to serious adverse reactions in dogs, so a vet-prescribed option is the safer route.

Most hot spots start improving within 48 hours of treatment and resolve in one to two weeks. If yours isn't improving in three days, call the vet back. There may be a deeper issue — a foreign body, a resistant infection, or an underlying endocrine disease like hypothyroidism or Cushing's.

Preventing the Next One

Once you've dealt with one hot spot, you'll do almost anything to avoid another. Here's what actually works.

Dry your dog thoroughly after every swim or bath. Towel dry, then use a forced-air dryer on thick-coated breeds. Pay attention to the armpits, groin, neck, and tail base. If you can feel dampness against the skin, you're not done.

Keep up with flea prevention year-round. Not just in summer. Flea allergies are the single most common trigger, and a missed dose in January can still cause a hot spot in a heated house.

Brush regularly and deal with mats immediately. Matting pulls at the skin, and the itch starts right there. For double-coated breeds, a good undercoat rake is worth its weight in gold. This one has held up well for me: undercoat rake for double-coated dogs.

Manage allergies aggressively. If your dog itches seasonally, talk to your vet about antihistamines, Apoquel, Cytopoint, or immunotherapy. Controlling the itch is how you prevent the hot spot.

Check your dog over weekly. Run your hands over their whole body. You'll find small spots before they become big ones. Takes two minutes.

Address boredom. A tired dog doesn't lick compulsively. More walks, more sniff work, more chew toys. I'm a big fan of snuffle mats for this — they burn mental energy fast, which is what anxious lickers actually need. Here's one that's survived a year with my two dogs: snuffle mat for dogs.

Keep the collar clean and dry. A wet collar against the neck is a classic hot spot setup. Rotate collars, wash them, or take them off when the dog swims.

When It's Not a Hot Spot

A few things look like hot spots but aren't, and treating them wrong makes things worse.

Ringworm. A fungal infection that can look like a circular, crusty, hairless patch. It's contagious to humans. Needs antifungal treatment, not antibiotics.

Mange. Demodex or sarcoptic mange causes hair loss, crusting, and intense itching. Sarcoptic mange is contagious to people. Needs a vet diagnosis and specific treatment.

Skin fold dermatitis. Common in bulldogs, pugs, and shar-peis. It happens in the folds, not on flat skin, and needs a different approach.

Anal gland abscess. If the swelling is right next to the anus, that's not a hot spot. It needs to be drained by a vet.

Insect bite or sting reaction. Usually smaller, with a visible puncture or swelling, and no matted fur over a weeping sore.

If you're not sure, don't guess. A vet visit costs less than a week of wrong treatment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use human antibiotic ointment on a dog hot spot? No. Neosporin and similar products contain ingredients dogs shouldn't ingest, and they're not formulated for canine skin. Use a vet-recommended product.

How fast do hot spots spread? Fast. A small spot can double in size in 12 hours and reach palm-sized in 24 to 48 hours if the dog keeps scratching. Speed of treatment is everything.

Are hot spots contagious to other dogs? The underlying trigger usually isn't, but the bacteria involved can spread to broken skin on other pets. Keep the affected dog's bedding separate until it heals.

Can I just leave it alone? No. Hot spots don't self-resolve. They get bigger, deeper, and more painful. Untreated, they can turn into deep pyoderma that requires weeks of antibiotics.

Do hot spots come back in the same spot? Often, yes — especially if the underlying trigger (allergies, fleas, moisture) hasn't been addressed. That's your signal to dig deeper than the surface.

The Bottom Line

Hot spots are one of those problems where doing the right thing in the first hour saves you a week of misery. Clip the fur, clean with chlorhexidine, cone the dog, and call your vet. Don't wait, don't improvise with kitchen remedies, and don't assume it's just a scratch. If your dog gets them repeatedly, stop treating the spots and start treating the cause — allergies, fleas, moisture, or boredom. That's where the real fix lives. Your dog will thank you by not needing a cone ever again.

title: Senior Cat Care: 9 Everyday Adjustments That Actually Help
description: Learn 9 practical senior cat care adjustments: litter box changes, warmth, nutrition, vet labs, and more that help cats over 10 thrive.
content:
Your Cat Didn't Get Old Overnight — But It Feels Like It

I still remember the day I realized my cat Waffle had stopped jumping onto the kitchen counter. She was 13, and the counter had been her throne for a decade. One week she was up there knocking pens off the edge, and the next she was staring up at it like it was a cliff face. Nothing dramatic happened. No yowl, no limping. She just quietly stopped. That is how aging works in cats — it sneaks in through the side door while you are busy worrying about something else.

Cats are considered seniors around age 11, according to the American Association of Feline Practitioners, and they are geriatric by 15. But here is the thing that gets missed: a 12-year-old cat is not simply a slower version of a 6-year-old cat. Their physiology changes. Kidney function declines. Joint cartilage wears down. Muscle mass drops. Their senses dull. The cat that used to hear a can opener from three rooms away might now sleep through dinner prep entirely.

The good news is that most of these changes respond really well to small, cheap, unglamorous adjustments around the house. I have made every one of these changes for my own cats, and I have watched clients transform miserable old cats into comfortable ones with nothing more than a litter box swap and a heating pad. Here is what actually matters.

1. Lower the Litter Box Entry — This Is Non-Negotiable

Arthritis is wildly underdiagnosed in cats. A 2023 study in the Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery found radiographic evidence of degenerative joint disease in over 90 percent of cats over 12. That means almost every senior cat you meet has some degree of joint pain, whether they show it or not. And cats are masters at hiding it.

A high-sided litter box that requires a jump or a big step over the rim becomes a genuine obstacle. Your cat may start peeing on a bath mat, and you may assume it is behavioral when it is actually orthopedic. I have seen this go wrong a dozen times — owners spend months and hundreds of dollars on behavioral consults when the fix was a $12 shallow pan.

What to do: switch to a low-entry box with a rim no taller than 2 to 3 inches. If your cat has significant mobility issues, a simple baking pan or a puppy training tray works fine. Cut a doorway into the side of a covered box, or just remove the lid entirely. Keep the box on the same floor as your cat's main hangout spot — stairs become a real barrier.

If you want a box that is genuinely easy for older cats, this low-entry litter box has a shallow lip and a generous interior, which makes turning around less of a production. I like it because there is no lid to negotiate and the sides are low enough that a stiff cat can walk in without a hop.

2. Warmth Is Medicine for Old Joints

Senior cats run cold. Their circulation is less efficient, they carry less insulating fat, and their metabolism often slows. A 70-degree house that felt fine at age 5 can feel genuinely chilly at 15. Cold makes arthritic joints stiffer, which makes cats move less, which makes them stiffer still. It is a nasty spiral.

Give your cat a warm spot. A heated cat bed is the single most appreciated thing you can buy an old cat, in my experience. If you do not want to spend money, a folded fleece blanket on top of a radiator-adjacent chair works. So does a cardboard box lined with a wool sweater. Cats do not care about aesthetics.

One warning: if you use a heating pad designed for humans, never leave it on high and never let your cat lie on it unsupervised. Cats with reduced sensation can develop burns. Pet-specific heated beds are designed to reach only about 102 degrees Fahrenheit, which is roughly their natural body temperature, and they shut off automatically. That is the safe range.

3. Rethink the Food and Water Setup

Two things happen to senior cats at the bowl. First, they often cannot crouch comfortably to eat from a floor-level dish. Second, their sense of smell declines, which makes food less appetizing. A cat that cannot smell dinner may just walk away.

Raise the bowls. A simple stack of books under a shallow dish, or a proper elevated feeder, takes the strain off the neck and shoulders. I have watched cats start eating again within a day of having their bowl lifted 4 inches off the floor. It sounds too simple to matter. It matters.

Warm the food slightly, too — about 10 seconds in the microwave, stirred, and tested with your finger. Warming releases aroma, and aroma drives appetite. For water, a fountain often helps because moving water is more attractive to cats and encourages drinking, which is critical for aging kidneys. According to the ASPCA, chronic kidney disease affects a large percentage of senior cats, and hydration is one of the few things owners can control directly.

This elevated bowl set is the one I recommend most often. It is stable, the bowls are shallow enough that whiskers do not drag, and the height works for cats in the 8 to 15 pound range. Whisker fatigue is real, by the way — deep narrow bowls can make eating genuinely unpleasant for sensitive cats.

4. Add Night Lights and Reduce Startle Triggers

Senior cats frequently develop nuclear sclerosis, a cloudiness in the lens that looks like cataracts but is not the same thing. It reduces contrast vision, especially in low light. Your cat is not blind, but they are navigating a world that is dimmer and blurrier than it used to be.

Plug in a couple of night lights near the litter box, the food station, and the path between them. This is a tiny change that prevents a lot of middle-of-the-night confusion and howling — the kind that wakes you up at 3 a.m. and makes you wonder if something is wrong. Sometimes nothing is wrong. Your cat just cannot see well enough to feel confident, and they are calling out to locate you.

Also, stop rearranging furniture. Old cats rely on routine and spatial memory. Moving the couch two feet to the left is a minor inconvenience to you and a disorienting event to a 16-year-old cat with fading vision.

5. Groom Them More — They Cannot Keep Up

Old cats stop grooming effectively. It is not laziness. It hurts to twist around to reach the back, and arthritic spines do not bend the way they used to. The result is mats, dandruff, and a greasy coat that smells a bit off.

Brush your senior cat daily with a soft slicker brush or a rubber curry. Keep sessions short — 2 to 3 minutes is plenty. Pay attention to the lower back, the hindquarters, and the belly, which are the spots they cannot reach. If you find mats, do not cut them out with scissors. Cat skin is paper-thin and moves constantly. I have seen owners slice a cat open trying to remove a mat, and it is a vet visit every time. Use blunt-tipped grooming scissors or, better, let a groomer or vet tech handle dense mats.

Check the claws, too. Senior cats shed claw sheaths less effectively, so nails get thick, curved, and sometimes grow into the paw pad. Trim every 2 to 3 weeks, just the clear tips. If you can see the pink quick, stay well away from it.

6. Keep Them Mentally Sharp With Easy Wins

Cognitive dysfunction syndrome — basically feline dementia — affects a meaningful percentage of cats over 15. Signs include staring at walls, yowling at night, getting stuck in corners, and seeming to forget where the litter box is. It is heartbreaking and it is also somewhat manageable.

Keep their brain working, but make it easy. Puzzle feeders are great for young cats; for seniors, use a simple muffin tin with treats in a few cups, or scatter a handful of kibble on a snuffle mat. The goal is engagement without frustration. A cat that fails repeatedly at a hard puzzle will just stop trying, which is the opposite of what you want.

Interactive play still matters, but shorten the sessions. Two 5-minute wand sessions a day beats one 15-minute marathon for an old cat. Let them catch the toy often. Winning is the point.

7. Bloodwork Twice a Year, Not Once

Here is my strong opinion: every cat over 10 should get a senior blood panel every 6 months, not annually. Cats are notoriously good at masking illness until they are 70 percent into organ failure. A twice-yearly panel catches kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, and diabetes early — when they are manageable — instead of late, when they are emergencies.

The panel should include a complete blood count, a chemistry profile, a T4 thyroid test, and a urinalysis. Ask for a blood pressure check too. Hypertension is common in older cats and silently damages the kidneys, heart, and eyes. According to the AVMA, routine wellness screening is one of the highest-value things owners can do for aging pets, and I have seen it catch early kidney changes in cats that looked completely normal at home.

Yes, it costs money. It costs far less than treating a crisis at 2 a.m.

8. Watch the Weight — Both Directions

Weight loss in a senior cat is a red flag, not a normal part of aging. It can mean hyperthyroidism, kidney disease, diabetes, cancer, or dental disease. If your cat drops more than 5 percent of body weight in a few months, that is a vet visit. Weigh your cat monthly on a baby scale if you can. It is the cheapest early warning system you have.

Weight gain matters too. An overweight senior cat puts more load on arthritic joints and is at higher risk for diabetes. If your cat is carrying extra pounds, talk to your vet about a senior-appropriate diet before you just cut portions — seniors need adequate protein to maintain muscle mass, and generic light formulas can shortchange them.

Dental health deserves a mention here. Periodontal disease is extremely common in older cats and can make eating painful enough that they stop. If your cat is dropping food, chewing on one side, or has truly terrible breath, get the mouth checked. A dental cleaning under anesthesia is a real risk-benefit conversation for a 16-year-old cat, but it is a conversation worth having.

9. Set Up a Comfortable Base Camp

Old cats like their spots. Give them several. A soft bed in the sunniest window, another near you on the couch, a third in a quiet corner away from foot traffic and other pets. Cats in pain or feeling vulnerable want to be near their people but not in the middle of the action.

Ramps and steps help cats who still want to reach the couch or the bed but cannot jump. A sturdy ottoman placed as a halfway point often works as well as a commercial ramp. Test it yourself — if it wobbles under your hand, it will wobble under your cat, and they will not use it.

Keep resources spread out. One litter box per floor. Water in more than one room. An old cat with arthritis should never have to walk more than about 20 feet to reach what they need.

The Thing Nobody Tells You About Old Cats

Living with a senior cat is a different relationship than living with a young one. It is quieter. It is more about maintenance than adventure. There is a temptation to treat every change as decline, and that is not quite right either. I have watched 17-year-old cats start playing again after their arthritis was managed. I have watched cats who had not purred in months start purring on a heated bed.

The work is small and constant: lower the box, warm the bed, lift the bowl, book the labs, brush the fur. None of it is dramatic. All of it adds up. Start with the litter box and the warmth, because those two give you the biggest return for the least effort, and then work your way down the list. Your cat cannot tell you their knees hurt. You have to notice for them.

One last practical note: find a vet you trust before you need one urgently. Ask them directly how they handle senior cats, what diagnostics they recommend, and how they approach quality-of-life decisions. Having that relationship in place makes the hard days less chaotic. Your old cat has spent years reading your moods and adjusting to your schedule. This is the part where you return the favor.

title: Why Your Rabbit Isn't Eating: Stasis, Stress, and the 12-Hour Rule
description: A rabbit that stops eating is a medical emergency. Learn the early warning signs of GI stasis, what to do in the first 12 hours, and how to prevent it.
content:
The 12-Hour Rule That Saves Rabbit Lives

If your rabbit hasn't touched food in 12 hours, you don't have a picky eater. You have a potential emergency. I've watched too many owners wait 24, 36, even 48 hours because the rabbit was 'still hopping around' or 'seemed fine otherwise.' By the time they called, the rabbit was hypothermic and barely responsive. The window for easy treatment had closed.

Rabbits are prey animals. They hide pain and illness until they physically can't. A rabbit that stops eating is almost always already sick. And the number one cause of that sudden appetite loss is gastrointestinal stasis — a slowdown or complete halt of the gut. It kills fast. According to the ASPCA, GI stasis is one of the most common and most preventable causes of death in pet rabbits. The key word is preventable.

Let's talk about what's actually happening in your rabbit's gut, the early signs most owners miss, and the exact steps to take when you notice something's off. I'll also cover the feeding and habitat mistakes that trigger stasis in the first place, because most of what I see in practice is fixable with a few changes.

What GI Stasis Actually Is (And Why It's Different From Dog or Cat Vomiting)

Rabbits can't vomit. Their digestive system is a one-way tube designed for near-constant movement. The stomach empties into the small intestine, then the cecum — a fermentation vat the size of a small fist — then the colon, and out. Food moves through in roughly 4 to 6 hours under normal conditions. When that movement slows, everything backs up.

The cecum is where the magic happens. It's packed with beneficial bacteria that ferment fiber into volatile fatty acids, which your rabbit absorbs for energy. It also produces cecotropes — soft, nutrient-dense pellets your rabbit eats directly from its rear. Those cecotropes are not poop. They're a second pass at nutrition, and a rabbit that stops producing or eating them is in trouble.

When gut motility drops, several things happen at once. Gas builds up because bacteria keep fermenting without moving forward. The cecum's pH shifts, killing off good bacteria and letting harmful ones bloom. The rabbit feels bloated and nauseated, so it stops eating. That makes motility worse. That makes gas worse. It's a spiral, and it can go from mild to life-threatening in under 24 hours.

I've seen this go wrong in a rabbit that was 'fine this morning.' The owner came home at 6 p.m. to a rabbit pressed into a corner, grinding its teeth, and refusing even a strawberry. By midnight it was in surgery. Stasis doesn't wait for your schedule.

Early Warning Signs You Can Actually Catch

You need to know your rabbit's normal. How much hay does it eat in a day? How many poops in the litter box? What does it do when you walk in the room? If you can't answer those questions, start paying attention today. The earliest stasis signs are behavioral, not physical.

1. Smaller or fewer poops. This is the single most reliable early sign. Normal rabbit poop is round, uniform, and plentiful — a healthy adult produces 100 to 300 pellets a day. If you're seeing tiny, irregular, or string-of-pearls poops, motility is already compromised. Count for a day. If the number drops by half, call your vet.

2. Picking at food. A rabbit that normally attacks its greens and now nibbles half-heartedly is not being fussy. It's nauseated. Same with hay — if the hay rack is still full at the end of the day, that's a red flag.

3. Hunched posture. A rabbit in pain sits with its back arched, belly pressed to the floor, eyes half-closed. It looks like it's loafing, but the body language is different. A relaxed loaf has soft eyes and a normal ear position. A pained loaf is rigid.

4. Tooth grinding. Soft grinding while eating is normal. Loud, constant grinding — especially when the rabbit isn't eating — means severe pain. That's the rabbit equivalent of a person groaning through a kidney stone.

5. Reduced grooming. Rabbits are fastidious. A rabbit that stops cleaning its face or leaves its bottom messy is not feeling well. A messy bottom also attracts flies, which can lead to flystrike — a whole separate emergency.

6. Lethargy or hiding. A rabbit that normally greets you at the cage door and now stays in its hide is telling you something. Don't wait for it to 'come around.'

If you see two or more of these signs together, treat it as stasis until proven otherwise. Don't wait for a full 12 hours if the rabbit is obviously uncomfortable. The 12-hour rule is for the borderline cases — the rabbit that's a little off but still moving. For the obvious ones, call immediately.

What to Do in the First 12 Hours

First, call your vet. Not a general practice that 'sees rabbits sometimes' — an exotics vet or a rabbit-savvy vet. The House Rabbit Society maintains a directory, and your local rabbit rescue will know who's good. If it's after hours, call the emergency clinic and ask if they have a rabbit vet on call. Many don't. Know your options before you need them.

While you're waiting for the appointment, here's what you can do at home. This is not a substitute for veterinary care. It's what you do to keep the rabbit stable until you get there.

Offer warm water in a bowl. Not cold. Rabbits in stasis often become dehydrated and hypothermic. Warm water is more appealing and easier on the gut. If your rabbit won't drink, you can offer a small amount of unflavored Pedialyte via syringe — 5 to 10 mL at a time, slowly, into the side of the mouth. Never squirt straight down the throat. Rabbits can aspirate, and that's a fast track to pneumonia.

Keep the rabbit warm. Normal rabbit body temperature is 101 to 103 degrees Fahrenheit. A stasis rabbit can drop below 100. Use a SnuggleSafe or a rice sock heated in the microwave, wrapped in a towel, placed in one corner of the cage so the rabbit can move away if it gets too warm. Do not use a heating pad on high — rabbits can't regulate well and can burn themselves.

Gentle belly massage. With the rabbit on your lap or a towel, use two fingers to make small circles on the abdomen, starting near the ribs and working down. You're trying to move gas. If the rabbit tenses, grinds its teeth, or tries to bite, stop. That means it's painful, and you need the vet now.

Offer favorite greens. Not pellets, not treats. Fresh herbs — parsley, cilantro, basil — or a small piece of romaine. The smell can sometimes trigger eating. If the rabbit takes a bite, great. If not, don't force it. Forcing food into a rabbit with a full stomach can cause a rupture.

Do not give over-the-counter gas drops without vet guidance. Simethicone is sometimes used, but the dose matters, and it doesn't address the underlying motility issue. I've seen owners give it and feel reassured, then wait another day. That's the danger.

What the Vet Will Do

A good rabbit vet will start with a physical exam — palpating the abdomen for gas, checking hydration, taking temperature, listening to gut sounds with a stethoscope. They'll likely take X-rays to rule out a blockage. This is important: stasis and blockage look similar but are treated differently. If there's a physical obstruction, you can't just push motility drugs. Surgery may be needed.

If it's uncomplicated stasis, treatment usually includes subcutaneous fluids, a motility drug like metoclopramide or cisapride, pain relief (meloxicam is common), and sometimes a prokinetic. The vet may also give a dose of famotidine for stomach acid. Many rabbits go home the same day with oral meds and a feeding plan.

Critical care feeding is the next step. If the rabbit won't eat on its own, you'll syringe-feed a recovery formula like Oxbow Critical Care or Sherwood SARx. This is not optional. A rabbit's gut needs food moving through it to keep working. The vet will calculate how many milliliters per day based on weight — usually 15 to 30 mL per kilogram, split into 4 to 6 feedings. It's messy, it's slow, and it's the difference between recovery and losing the rabbit.

I recommend asking your vet to show you how to syringe-feed before you leave the clinic. Watching a video is not the same as doing it with a wiggly rabbit on your lap. Get hands-on instruction.

The Feeding Mistakes That Cause Stasis

Now the part most owners don't want to hear: stasis is often a husbandry problem. The rabbit didn't just 'get sick.' Something in its diet or environment set the stage.

Not enough hay. This is the big one. A rabbit's diet should be 80 to 90 percent grass hay — timothy, orchard, brome, or meadow. Hay provides the long-strand fiber that keeps the gut moving. A rabbit on a pellet-heavy diet is a rabbit on the fast track to stasis. Pellets are concentrated nutrition with short fiber. They're a supplement, not a base. An adult rabbit should get about 1/4 cup of plain pellets per 5 pounds of body weight per day, and unlimited hay.

Too many treats. Carrots, bananas, apples, yogurt drops — these are sugar bombs. Sugar feeds the wrong bacteria in the cecum and disrupts the pH. A small piece of carrot once or twice a week is fine. A handful every day is not. I've seen rabbits come in with stasis purely from a 'treat habit' the owner thought was harmless.

Sudden diet changes. Switching pellets or introducing a new green cold turkey can throw the gut off. Always transition over 7 to 10 days, mixing old and new. Same with new vegetables — one at a time, small amounts, watch the poop.

Dehydration. A rabbit that doesn't drink enough is a rabbit at risk. Water bottles are fine, but many rabbits drink more from a bowl. Offer both. Change the water daily. If your rabbit suddenly stops drinking, that's a warning sign on its own.

Stress, Pain, and Other Triggers

Diet is the main lever, but it's not the only one. Stress can trigger stasis in a rabbit with a perfectly good diet. Moving to a new home, losing a bonded mate, a predator in the yard, a loud construction project next door — all of these can shut down a rabbit's gut.

Pain is another trigger. Dental disease is a huge one. Rabbits' teeth grow continuously, and if they're not wearing down properly, they develop sharp points (spurs) that cut into the tongue and cheeks. A rabbit with dental pain stops eating, and then stasis sets in. If your rabbit is dropping food, drooling, or losing weight despite eating, get the teeth checked. According to the AVMA, dental disease is one of the top three health problems in pet rabbits, and it's often the hidden cause behind a stasis episode.

Other pain sources: urinary tract infections, arthritis in older rabbits, abscesses, and injuries. Any of these can put a rabbit off its food. The stasis is a symptom, not the root cause. Treating the stasis without addressing the pain is a temporary fix.

I had a case where a rabbit kept going into stasis every few weeks. Diet was perfect. Hay intake was great. Turned out the rabbit had a molar spur that was just bad enough to cause intermittent pain. Once the vet filed the teeth, the stasis stopped. That's the kind of thing you only find if you look.

Setting Up the Habitat to Prevent Stasis

Environment matters more than most owners realize. A rabbit that doesn't move doesn't poop. Exercise stimulates gut motility. A rabbit confined to a small cage all day is at higher risk.

Give your rabbit room to run. A minimum of 12 square feet of floor space for a single rabbit, plus supervised time outside the enclosure every day. If you can't free-roam, use an exercise pen. The goal is 3 to 4 hours of active time daily. That's not a lot. A bored rabbit is a static rabbit.

Enrichment also matters. Foraging toys, cardboard boxes to shred, tunnels to run through — these encourage movement and natural behaviors. A rabbit that's mentally engaged is a rabbit that's physically active. I've had good luck with simple things: a paper bag stuffed with hay, a untreated wicker basket, a stack of towels to dig in. You don't need to buy much.

Water access is critical. I recommend both a bowl and a bottle. Bowls are more natural and encourage drinking, but bottles stay cleaner. Having both gives your rabbit options and lets you monitor intake. If the bowl is empty every morning and the bottle is untouched, you know your rabbit is drinking. If both are full, you have a problem.

Monitoring: The Daily Five-Minute Check

You don't need to be a vet to catch stasis early. You need a routine. I tell every rabbit owner to do a five-minute check every morning and every evening. It's not obsessive. It's how you catch problems before they become emergencies.

Morning: Look at the litter box. Are the poops normal in size, shape, and number? Fill the hay rack. Did the rabbit eat overnight? Offer a small handful of greens. Does the rabbit come over? Check the water bowl. Is it lower than yesterday?

Evening: Same routine. Look at the rabbit. Is it moving normally? Grooming? Interested in its surroundings? Feel the belly gently — is it soft or tense? A normal rabbit belly feels like a soft dough. A gassy belly feels tight and may make a hollow sound when you tap it.

Write it down if you have to. A simple note on your phone with the date and a checkmark for 'normal' or a note about what was off. Patterns emerge. You'll notice a day where the rabbit ate less hay, or the poops were smaller, and you can act before it's a crisis.

When to Call the Vet Immediately (No Waiting)

Call now, not in the morning, if you see any of these:

  • No eating for 12 hours or more
  • No poop for 12 hours or more
  • Lying on the side, unresponsive
  • Labored breathing
  • Cold ears and feet (temperature under 100°F)
  • Loud, constant tooth grinding
  • Bloated, drum-tight abdomen
  • Collapse or seizures

These are late-stage signs. The rabbit needs emergency care, not a wait-and-see approach. If your regular vet can't see you, call the nearest emergency clinic and ask specifically if they have a veterinarian experienced with rabbits. Not all do. If they don't, ask for a referral. Drive an hour if you have to. Stasis at this stage is a race.

Recovery: What the Next Two Weeks Look Like

If you caught it early and the vet treated it, recovery is usually straightforward. The rabbit gets fluids, motility drugs, pain meds, and syringe feeding until it starts eating on its own. That can take 3 to 7 days. The first sign of improvement is usually poop — small at first, then bigger and more regular. Appetite comes back gradually. Don't rush it.

Keep the rabbit warm, quiet, and stress-free. Limit handling to feeding and meds. Offer hay constantly, even if the rabbit ignores it. Offer greens multiple times a day. Fresh water in a bowl. No treats until the rabbit is fully back to normal. I know it's tempting to celebrate with a carrot, but sugar is the last thing a recovering gut needs.

After the episode, do a full husbandry review. What was the diet? What was the stress? What was the hay quality? If you can't identify a cause, assume it's diet and fix the hay-to-pellet ratio anyway. Most rabbits improve on a hay-first diet. I've seen rabbits go from monthly stasis episodes to zero after switching to unlimited timothy hay and cutting pellets to a measured 1/4 cup.

One thing I've learned the hard way: don't assume the problem is solved just because the rabbit is eating again. The underlying cause is still there unless you fix it. I've seen rabbits relapse within a month because the owner went back to the old feeding routine. Stasis is a symptom. Treat the symptom, then treat the cause.

The Bottom Line

Your rabbit's gut is a delicate, fast-moving system that depends on constant fiber intake. When it stops, the clock starts. Know the early signs — smaller poops, picking at food, hunched posture — and act on them. Don't wait for the dramatic symptoms. By then, you've lost time you can't get back.

Feed hay first, always. Keep water available in a bowl. Give your rabbit room to run. Do the five-minute check twice a day. And find a rabbit-savvy vet before you need one. That's the whole game. Do those things and you'll likely never see stasis. If you do see it, you'll know exactly what to do.

title: Why Is My Aquarium Water Cloudy? The 7 Causes and Exactly How to Fix Each One
description: Cloudy aquarium water isn't one problem — it's seven. Learn to identify bacterial blooms, green water, and milky haze, then fix each one properly.
content:
Cloudy Water Is a Symptom, Not a Diagnosis

I've lost count of how many times a new fishkeeper has sent me a photo of a milky tank with the same message: 'I did a water change and it got worse.' That's the tell. If a water change makes the cloudiness worse, you're not dealing with dirt. You're dealing with a biological bloom, and fighting it with more water changes is like bailing out a boat while the tap is still running.

Cloudy water in a freshwater aquarium has roughly seven distinct causes, and they look similar enough that most people misdiagnose them. Milky white haze from a bacterial bloom is a completely different problem from pea-soup green water, which is different again from the grey-brown tint that comes from stirred-up substrate. Treat the wrong one and you'll spend three weeks and a lot of money chasing your tail.

This guide walks through each cause in the order you're most likely to encounter it, how to confirm it's actually what you think it is, and the specific fix. No product roundups. Just the diagnosis and the work.

First: Rule Out the Obvious

Before you diagnose anything biological, check three mechanical things. I've seen experienced keepers miss these because they assumed the problem was chemistry.

Stirred-up substrate. If you just added new sand or gravel and didn't rinse it thoroughly, that fine particulate will hang in the water column for days. It looks like a grey-white haze and it settles on every surface. Test: turn off your filter for an hour. If the water clears noticeably from the top down, it's particulate, not biological. Fix: mechanical filtration with fine filter floss, and rinse any new substrate under running water until the runoff is clear before it ever touches the tank — I mean twenty minutes of rinsing, not two.

Filter malfunction. A clogged impeller or a filter that's lost prime will stop moving water, and stagnant water goes cloudy fast. Check that water is actually flowing out of the return. If your canister filter is gurgling, it's got air in it and you need to reprime it.

Dead fish or decaying matter. A fish that died behind the rocks will spike ammonia and trigger a bacterial bloom within 24 hours. Do a headcount. Check behind decor, inside caves, and around filter intakes. I once found a dead pleco wedged behind a heater that had been there for three days and turned a 75-gallon tank into milk.

If all three check out, you're dealing with one of the seven causes below.

Cause 1: Bacterial Bloom (Milky White Haze)

This is the single most common cause of cloudy water in a new tank, and it's also the most misunderstood. The water looks like someone poured milk into it. It's white or slightly grey, it doesn't clear with water changes, and it often shows up 3 to 10 days after setup.

What's happening is a heterotrophic bacteria bloom. These are the bacteria that break down organic waste, and they reproduce explosively when there's a sudden food source. In a new tank, that food source is the organic matter leaching from your substrate, your plants, and your tap water. The bacteria multiply so fast that they become visible in the water column — each milliliter can contain millions of cells.

Here's the counterintuitive part: a bacterial bloom is a sign your tank is cycling correctly. It's not a disease. The bloom will clear on its own in 3 to 7 days as the bacteria consume the available food and die back. What kills fish during a bloom isn't the cloudiness — it's the oxygen depletion. Those billions of bacteria are consuming oxygen, and in a warm tank with poor surface agitation, dissolved oxygen can crash.

The fix: Increase surface agitation. Point a powerhead or filter return at the surface to create ripples. Add an air stone if you don't have one. Don't do large water changes — that just resets the cycle and prolongs the bloom. Small 10 to 15 percent changes every other day are fine if fish are gasping. And critically, don't add more fish or overfeed during this period.

If the bloom hasn't cleared after 10 days, you've got a persistent organic source. Check for decaying plant matter, uneaten food, or a dead fish you missed.

Cause 2: Green Water (Algae Bloom)

Green water is a free-floating algae bloom, usually single-celled chlorophytes that multiply in the water column. It's distinct from the algae that grows on glass and decor — this stuff makes the entire tank look like pea soup, and it can get so dense that you can't see your fish from six inches away.

The cause is almost always an excess nutrient combined with too much light. Specifically: ammonia or nitrate above 20 ppm, plus 10 or more hours of light per day, plus phosphate from overfeeding or tap water. Green water is the classic symptom of a tank that's getting too much food and too much light.

I've seen green water appear overnight in tanks where the owner was feeding three times a day and leaving the light on for 12 hours. The algae had everything it needed.

The fix: This is the one cause where you need to attack on multiple fronts simultaneously. First, black out the tank completely for 3 to 5 days. Wrap it in a blanket or towel so no light gets in. Feed nothing during this period — fish can go a week without food easily. Second, do a 50 percent water change at the end of the blackout. Third, reduce your photoperiod to 6 to 8 hours per day and feed once daily, only what the fish consume in two minutes. Fourth, test your tap water for phosphate and nitrate. If your tap water comes out at 20 ppm nitrate, you're fighting a losing battle with water changes alone and need to consider a different water source or a nitrate-removing filter media.

An ultraviolet sterilizer will clear green water in 3 to 5 days and is the fastest mechanical fix. But if you don't address the nutrient and light imbalance, it comes right back. I've watched people run UV continuously for months because they never fixed the root cause.

Cause 3: Yellow or Tea-Colored Water (Tannins)

If your water looks like weak tea or apple juice, you've got tannins. These come from driftwood, Indian almond leaves, peat, and some botanical additives. Tannins are not harmful — in fact, they have mild antibacterial and antifungal properties, and many South American fish like tetras and discus actually prefer blackwater conditions.

But if you didn't intend to have tannins, they're annoying. The water is clear, just tinted. It doesn't look cloudy in the milky sense.

The fix: If you don't want the tint, remove the wood and boil it for an hour, then soak it in fresh water for a week, changing the water daily until it runs clear. Even then, some wood leaches for months. A quality activated carbon in your filter will pull tannins out of the water column and needs replacing every 3 to 4 weeks while the wood is still leaching. If you have a lot of wood, expect this to be a months-long process.

Personally, I've stopped fighting tannins. They're beneficial for most community fish, and a slight amber tint looks natural. But if you're keeping fish that prefer hard, clear water like African cichlids, tannins are a problem and you need to remove the source.

Cause 4: White, Stringy Cloudiness (Diatoms)

Diatoms look like a brown or greyish-white film on glass, substrate, and decor, and they can make the water look dusty. They're most common in new tanks between weeks 2 and 8, and in tanks with high silicate levels.

Diatoms are actually a normal part of tank maturation. They consume silicates from the water and substrate, and once the silicate is used up, they die off on their own. The key is not to panic and not to over-clean.

The fix: Wait it out. Diatoms disappear in 2 to 4 weeks in most tanks. Snails — especially nerites — and otocinclus catfish will graze them down. If the tank is older than 3 months and you still have diatoms, check your tap water for silicate, which is common in some municipal supplies and in sandblasting sand used as substrate. Rinsing new substrate more thoroughly helps, and removing silica-based sand is the long-term fix if your tap water is the source.

Cause 5: Grey or Brown Haze That Clears From the Top Down

This is particulate matter — fine debris that's suspended in the water column. It's almost always mechanical, not biological. Sources include unrinsed substrate, filter media that's breaking down, decaying plant matter, and the dust that comes off some aquarium rocks during initial setup.

The diagnostic test is simple: turn off all flow for an hour. If the water clears from the top down, leaving a layer of debris on the bottom, it's particulate. If it stays uniformly hazy, it's biological.

The fix: Mechanical filtration with progressively finer media. Start with coarse sponge, then filter floss, then a polishing pad. Clean or replace the floss every 2 to 3 days until the water clears. A diatom filter or a filter packed with filter floss will polish 100 gallons of water in a few hours. Don't vacuum the substrate aggressively during this period — you'll just stir up more.

Cause 6: Cloudy Water After a Water Change

If the water goes cloudy within hours of a water change, you've either disturbed the substrate or shocked the bacterial colony. The second one is more common than people realize.

When you do a large water change with water that's significantly different in temperature, pH, or hardness, the beneficial bacteria in your filter can go dormant or die off partially. That causes an ammonia spike, which triggers a bacterial bloom, which causes cloudiness. This is why I tell people never to do more than a 50 percent water change at once, and to match temperature within 2 degrees Fahrenheit and to dechlorinate before the water goes in, not after.

If your tap water has chloramine rather than chlorine, standard dechlorinators that only bind chlorine will leave the ammonia component behind. That ammonia feeds a bloom. You need a conditioner that specifically binds chloramine — most modern ones do, but check the label.

The fix: Stop doing large water changes. Do 20 percent changes every 3 to 4 days until the bloom clears. Match temperature precisely. Use a conditioner that handles chloramine. And don't clean your filter media in tap water during this period — rinse it in tank water you've removed, or you'll kill the bacteria you're trying to preserve.

Cause 7: Persistent Cloudiness With No Obvious Cause

Sometimes the water is cloudy, all your parameters look fine, and nothing you do helps. When I hit this wall, it's almost always one of three things.

Overstocking. If your tank has more fish than the filter can process, you'll have a chronic low-level bacterial bloom that never fully clears. The fix is a bigger filter, more frequent water changes, or fewer fish. There's no chemical that solves an overcrowded tank.

Overfeeding. Uneaten food decays and feeds bacteria. Feed only what the fish consume in 2 minutes, once or twice a day. If food hits the substrate, you're feeding too much. I've seen tanks clear up in a week just from cutting food in half.

Dead spots in filtration. If your filter is running but the flow isn't reaching all parts of the tank, you'll get localized stagnation and blooms. Add a powerhead or reposition the return to eliminate dead zones.

What About Chemical Clarifiers?

You'll see products that claim to clear cloudy water in hours by clumping particles together so the filter can catch them. They work — for particulate cloudiness. They do nothing for bacterial blooms, green water, or tannins, and using them repeatedly can stress fish by coating their gills. I keep a bottle on hand for polishing after a substrate disturbance, and that's it. They're a bandage, not a cure.

The same goes for 'cloudy water' products that claim to add beneficial bacteria. If you're mid-cycle, they might help seed the colony. If you're dealing with an established bloom, adding more bacteria doesn't fix the underlying nutrient imbalance.

The Diagnostic Cheat Sheet

Here's the short version I give people who message me with a photo and no other information.

Milky white, new tank, doesn't clear with water changes — bacterial bloom. Increase oxygen, wait it out, don't overfeed.

Pea green, visibility under 6 inches — algae bloom. Blackout 3 to 5 days, reduce light to 6 to 8 hours, cut feeding, test for nitrate and phosphate.

Tea-colored but clear — tannins. Remove or boil wood, run carbon, or accept it as beneficial.

Brown film on surfaces plus dusty water — diatoms. Wait 2 to 4 weeks, add snails, check silicate.

Grey haze that settles when flow stops — particulate. Mechanical filtration with fine floss, rinse new substrate better.

Cloudy within hours of a water change — bacterial shock or chloramine. Match temperature, use the right conditioner, do smaller changes.

Persistent low-level haze with good parameters — overstocking, overfeeding, or dead spots. Fix the husbandry, not the water.

When Cloudy Water Is Actually an Emergency

Cloudy water itself rarely kills fish. What kills fish is what's causing it. If your fish are gasping at the surface, that's an oxygen emergency — increase surface agitation immediately and do a 25 percent water change with temperature-matched, dechlorinated water. If your ammonia or nitrite is above 0.5 ppm, you've got a toxicity problem and need daily 25 to 50 percent water changes until it drops. If fish are lethargic, losing color, or developing red streaks, you're looking at a bacterial infection secondary to poor water quality and you need to test everything and possibly treat the tank.

According to the ASPCA, poor water quality is one of the leading contributors to disease in aquarium fish, and ammonia and nitrite toxicity are the most common culprits. That's worth repeating: the cloudiness is a signal, and the signal is usually telling you your nitrogen cycle is out of balance.

What I Actually Do

When I see cloudy water in one of my tanks, I don't reach for a product. I test ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate first. That tells me whether I'm dealing with a cycle problem or a nutrient problem. Then I look at the color. White means bacteria. Green means algae. Brown means diatoms or particulate. Tea means tannins.

Ninety percent of the time, the fix is the same: feed less, light less, increase oxygen, and stop doing large water changes. The other ten percent is a specific mechanical issue — unrinsed substrate or a dead fish — that I find by looking harder.

If you take one thing from this, let it be this: cloudy water is your tank telling you something is out of balance. The answer is almost never a bottle. It's a change in how you're running the tank. Fix the cause and the cloudiness clears. Chase the cloudiness and you'll be back here in a month with the same photo.

title: Reptile Brumation vs Hibernation: What's Actually Happening and How to Manage It Safely
description: Brumation isn't hibernation. Learn what's happening in your reptile's body, which species do it, and how to manage it without risking their life.
content:
Your Bearded Dragon Just Slept for Three Days Straight — Now What?

You check the enclosure. Eyes closed. Breathing so slow you have to stare at the ribcage for a full minute to confirm it's still happening. Food bowl untouched. You poke the tail. Nothing. This is the moment most new reptile keepers panic and start Googling 'is my bearded dragon dead' at 2 a.m.

I've been there. A decade ago I rushed a perfectly healthy adult male beardie to an emergency vet in January because he'd gone dark and limp under his hide. The vet — an actual reptile vet, not the dog-and-cat guy down the street — looked at me, looked at the lizard, and said: 'He's brumating. Take him home. Stop warming him up.' That $180 lesson is why I'm writing this.

Brumation and hibernation get used interchangeably in pet forums. They are not the same thing. Not even close. And how you handle the difference can mean the difference between a reptile that wakes up in March lean but healthy, and one that never wakes up at all.

What Brumation Actually Is (And Why It Isn't Hibernation)

Hibernation is a mammalian strategy. Bears, groundhogs, bats — they drop their body temperature dramatically, slow their metabolism by up to 90%, and survive off stored fat for months. Their bodies are built for it. A bear's heart can drop to 8 beats per minute and it just... works.

Brumation is the reptile and amphibian version, but it operates differently. Reptiles are ectotherms — their body temperature is dictated by their environment. They can't generate internal heat to keep organs functioning during a deep freeze. So instead of a true hibernation, brumation is a period of reduced activity, reduced feeding, and reduced metabolism triggered by cooler temperatures, shorter photoperiods (day length), and barometric pressure changes.

Here's the part that matters: brumating reptiles still need to drink. They still need to breathe. They still need to thermoregulate occasionally. A brumating reptile that gets too cold for too long doesn't wake up. It dies. According to the ASPCA, reptiles in brumation should be monitored regularly and kept within a safe temperature range specific to their species — never allowed to freeze.

So when someone tells you 'just let him sleep, it's natural,' they're half right. It is natural. But 'natural' in a glass box in your living room is not the same as 'natural' in the wild, where a lizard can dig deeper, find a warmer microclimate, or move if conditions go wrong.

Which Reptiles Brumate (And Which Don't)

Not every reptile brumates. This is where people get into trouble — they assume their tropical species should slow down in winter, drop the temps, and accidentally kill it.

Species that commonly brumate in captivity:

  • Bearded dragons (especially adults)
  • Blue-tongue skinks
  • Uromastyx
  • Russian tortoises, Hermann's tortoises, Greek tortoises
  • Corn snakes, king snakes, milk snakes (many colubrids)
  • Ball pythons (sometimes, but often a partial slowdown rather than true brumation)
  • Box turtles

Species that do NOT brumate and should never be cooled for it:

  • Leopard geckos (they slow down with cooler temps but don't truly brumate — a 'cooling period' is for breeding, not survival)
  • Crested geckos
  • Most tropical geckos
  • Green iguanas
  • Chameleons
  • Most aquatic turtles kept indoors
  • Monitor lizards (with a few exceptions)

If you're not sure whether your species brumates, don't guess. Check a species-specific care sheet from a reputable source or ask an exotics vet. I've seen keepers drop temps on a crested gecko because 'it's winter' and end up with a respiratory infection that took three months and two vet visits to clear.

The Physiology: What's Happening Inside Your Reptile

When a bearded dragon enters brumation, several things happen at once:

Metabolism drops. Digestive enzymes slow dramatically. This is why feeding a brumating reptile is dangerous — food sits in the gut and rots. That's how you get impaction, sepsis, and death. I've seen this go wrong with a corn snake that was fed 'just one more mouse' before a planned cooldown. The mouse didn't digest. The snake didn't make it.

Heart rate drops. A resting bearded dragon might have a heart rate around 60 bpm. During deep brumation, it can drop to 10 or lower. You can't hear it with a stethoscope unless you know what you're doing.

Immune function changes. White blood cell activity decreases. A reptile that goes into brumation with a latent infection often wakes up with a full-blown one. This is why a pre-brumation vet check is worth the money.

Hormonal shifts. For many species, brumation is tied to reproductive cycling. Males produce sperm more actively after a cool period. Females follicle up. If you're breeding, brumation is often part of the protocol. If you're not breeding, it's still going to happen for many species whether you plan for it or not.

According to peer-reviewed research published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, brumation in reptiles is not simply a passive response to cold — it's an actively regulated state involving gene expression changes that protect organs during low-oxygen and low-temperature conditions. Your reptile isn't just 'sleeping.' Its body is running a completely different operating system.

Signs Your Reptile Is Entering Brumation

Brumation doesn't happen overnight. It's a gradual slide that can take two to four weeks. Watch for:

  • Refusing food (the first and most obvious sign)
  • Spending more time on the cool side of the enclosure
  • Retreating to a hide and staying there
  • Eyes closed more often, even during the day
  • Slower response to handling or movement
  • Bowel movements becoming infrequent or stopping
  • Color darkening in some species (beardies often go darker)

What brumation is NOT:

  • Sudden collapse or unresponsiveness (that's an emergency)
  • Gasping, wheezing, or open-mouth breathing (respiratory infection)
  • Weight loss despite eating (parasites or illness)
  • Lethargy with normal appetite (something else is wrong)

If your reptile stops eating but is still active, basking normally, and losing weight, that's not brumation. That's a vet visit.

How to Manage Brumation: The Step-by-Step Protocol

You don't have to force brumation. If your reptile's temps stay stable and day length stays long, many species will skip it or do a very mild version. But if your house gets cold in winter, or if you have a species that strongly cycles, you need a plan.

Step 1: Pre-Brumation Vet Check (2-4 Weeks Before)

Get a fecal float and a basic physical. You're looking for parasites, respiratory sounds, and overall body condition. A reptile that goes into brumation with a parasite load can crash hard. If your vet finds something, treat it first. Brumation is not the time for medical drama.

Step 2: Stop Feeding at the Right Time

This is the step people screw up most. You need to stop feeding early enough that the digestive tract is completely empty before temps drop. For most lizards, that's 2 weeks. For snakes, 2-3 weeks. For tortoises, 3-4 weeks.

How do you know the gut is empty? You see a final bowel movement. No poop, no brumation. Keep the basking spot at normal temps during this fasting period so digestion finishes properly.

My rule: if I haven't seen a poop in the 7 days before I plan to start cooling, I delay the whole process. Better to skip brumation for a year than risk a rotting gut.

Step 3: Gradually Reduce Temperatures

Don't drop from 105°F basking to 75°F overnight. That's a shock. Drop the basking spot by about 5°F every 3-4 days, and let the ambient cool side drop by 2-3°F per week.

For a bearded dragon, a typical brumation target is:

  • Basking spot: 75-80°F (down from 100-105°F)
  • Cool side: 65-70°F
  • Night drop: no lower than 60°F

For a corn snake:

  • Warm side: 70-75°F
  • Cool side: 55-60°F
  • Never below 50°F

For a Russian tortoise:

  • Ambient: 50-60°F
  • Never below 40°F

These are starting points, not gospel. Adjust based on your species and your vet's advice.

Step 4: Reduce Photoperiod

Drop your light cycle from 12 hours on to 10, then 8, then 6 over the same 3-4 week period. Use a timer. Don't eyeball it. A $15 timer prevents a lot of problems.

If you use UVB, keep it on during the reduced photoperiod. Brumating reptiles still benefit from low-level UVB exposure, especially if they wake up and bask for a few hours. Turn it off entirely only if your species is a true burrower that stays underground for months.

Step 5: Monitor Weight and Hydration

Weigh your reptile weekly on a digital kitchen scale. A healthy brumating reptile should lose no more than 5-10% of its body weight over the entire brumation period. If it drops more than that, wake it up and call your vet.

Offer a shallow water dish at all times. Some reptiles will drink during brumation; most won't. But the option needs to be there. For snakes, I've had good luck with a quick soak every 3-4 weeks — just 10 minutes in lukewarm water to encourage drinking and a bowel movement.

Step 6: Wake-Up Protocol

When your reptile starts moving around on its own — usually in late February or March for temperate species — reverse the process. Raise temps by 5°F every few days. Increase photoperiod by an hour every few days. Offer food only after the basking spot is back to normal and you've seen the reptile actively basking for at least two days.

Start with small meals. One small roach instead of a full bowl. One small mouse instead of a large rat. The digestive system needs to wake up too.

What Can Go Wrong (And How to Prevent It)

Respiratory infection. Cool, damp conditions plus a compromised immune system equals trouble. Keep the enclosure dry during brumation. If you see bubbles around the nose or hear clicking, wake the reptile up and get to a vet.

Dehydration. Brumating reptiles can dehydrate slowly over months. A water dish and occasional soaks prevent this. If your reptile's eyes look sunken or the skin tents when pinched, it's dehydrated.

Impaction from undigested food. Already covered, but it's worth repeating: no food in the gut before cooling. Ever.

Getting too cold. If your power goes out in a cold snap and your enclosure drops below safe minimums, you need a backup heat source. A battery-powered heat mat or a few hand warmers wrapped in a towel can buy you time. According to the AVMA, prolonged exposure to temperatures below a species' critical thermal minimum can cause organ failure and death.

Waking up too early. If your reptile wakes in January because your house got warm, don't panic. Offer water. Offer a small meal if it's actively basking. Then let it decide whether to go back down. Forcing it back into brumation after a wake-up is stressful and often unsuccessful.

Do You Have to Brumate?

No. For most pet reptiles, brumation is optional. If you keep temperatures and lighting stable year-round, many species will skip it entirely or do a mild slowdown. This is especially true for captive-bred animals that have never experienced a true winter.

That said, some species seem to benefit from it. Breeding adults often need a cool period to cycle properly. And some keepers report that brumation leads to stronger appetite and more active behavior in spring.

My take: if your reptile is healthy, you have the setup to control temps precisely, and you're willing to monitor closely, brumation is fine. If your reptile is young, underweight, recovering from illness, or you're not confident in your temperature control, skip it. A year without brumation is not a problem. A botched brumation can be fatal.

If you're considering breeding, pick up a quality temperature controller and a reliable digital hygrometer/thermometer combo. I've used the Inkbird ITC-308 temperature controller for years on brumation setups — it holds temps within a degree or two and has saved me from a power-outage disaster more than once. For monitoring, the Govee Bluetooth hygrometer thermometer lets you check conditions from your phone without opening the enclosure and disturbing a sleeping reptile.

Species-Specific Notes

Bearded dragons: Adults often brumate for 2-4 months. Juveniles under a year should not be brumated — they need calories for growth. If a juvenile tries to brumate, check temps and lighting first. Often it's a husbandry issue, not a natural cycle.

Ball pythons: Many ball pythons go off food in winter without true brumation. This is a 'winter fast' rather than brumation. Keep temps normal, offer food weekly, and don't panic. A healthy ball python can fast for months without issue. If you're breeding, a 2-3 month cool period at 75-78°F is common.

Russian tortoises: These guys brumate hard in the wild. In captivity, you can either brumate them properly (50-60°F for 8-12 weeks) or keep them awake with consistent heat and light. Both are valid. What's not valid is letting them get cold and damp — that's how you get respiratory infections.

Corn snakes: Easy brumators. 55-60°F for 8-12 weeks is standard for breeding. Non-breeding corns can skip it with no issues.

Leopard geckos: Do not brumate. They may slow down with cooler temps, but they should always have access to a warm spot and should not be cooled below 70°F. A 'cooling period' for breeding is different — that's a slight temp drop with continued feeding, not a true brumation.

Frequently Asked Brumation Questions

How long does brumation last? Anywhere from 4 weeks to 5 months, depending on species, age, and conditions. Bearded dragons typically go 2-4 months. Tortoises can go 3-5 months. Snakes usually 2-3 months.

Should I handle a brumating reptile? Minimally. A quick weekly weight check is fine. Otherwise, leave it alone. Handling wakes them up, burns calories, and stresses the system.

What if my reptile wakes up in the middle of brumation? Let it bask. Offer water. If it's active for more than a day, offer a small meal. It may go back down or it may be done. Follow its lead.

Can I brumate a sick reptile? Absolutely not. Brumation suppresses the immune system. A sick reptile needs heat, food, and veterinary care, not a cooldown.

Do I need to brumate my reptile to breed it? For many species, yes — a cool period triggers reproductive cycling. For others, no. Research your specific species. If you're not breeding, brumation is optional.

The Bottom Line

Brumation is not hibernation. It's a controlled slowdown, not a deep freeze. Your reptile is still alive, still breathing, still needs water, and still needs you to pay attention.

If you're going to brumate, do it right: vet check first, empty the gut, drop temps gradually, monitor weight weekly, and wake up slowly. If you're not confident in any of those steps, don't do it. A reptile that skips brumation for a year is fine. A reptile that brumates badly is dead.

And if you ever find yourself staring at a motionless lizard at 2 a.m. wondering if it's dead — check for breathing, check the temperature, and call a reptile vet before you do anything drastic. I learned that lesson the expensive way so you don't have to.

For a reliable way to track temps during brumation, the Zoo Med digital thermometer is a solid budget option that I've used in multiple enclosures. And for keeping your brumation setup clean and safe, the F10SC veterinary disinfectant is the gold standard — it's what my vet uses.
